    18 — Global decorations: night, distortion and tiles¶

    Three decorations that belong to the whole globe rather than to a data layer: nightshade shades the night side at an instant, tissot makes a projection's distortion visible, and basemap pulls XYZ tiles in under the map.

    API: Map.nightshade, Map.tissot, Map.basemap.

    Where this data comes from. Everything in this notebook is real, downloaded with earthlens and committed under examples/data/: WorldPop population grids, OpenStreetMap roads, GBIF bird occurrences and geoBoundaries admin polygons. examples/data/ATTRIBUTION.md records each source and its licence.

    Setup — plus datetime, which nightshade needs.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    %matplotlib inline
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pyramids.dataset import Dataset
from pyramids.feature import FeatureCollection

from digitalearth.static import Map

# The notebook's own folder is the kernel's working directory, so the bundled
# example data sits two levels up: docs/examples -> repo root.
DATA = Path("../../examples/data")

# UTM zone 32N: a metric CRS, correct for south-west Germany.
UTM32 = 25832

import datetime as dt
    %matplotlib inline from pathlib import Path import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from pyramids.dataset import Dataset from pyramids.feature import FeatureCollection from digitalearth.static import Map # The notebook's own folder is the kernel's working directory, so the bundled # example data sits two levels up: docs/examples -> repo root. DATA = Path("../../examples/data") # UTM zone 32N: a metric CRS, correct for south-west Germany. UTM32 = 25832 import datetime as dt

    nightshade — the terminator at an instant¶

    nightshade(when) shades the hemisphere in darkness at a given moment. Pass a timezone-aware datetime: the terminator's position depends on the exact instant, so a naive one is an invitation to be an hour out.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    solstice_noon = dt.datetime(2026, 6, 21, 12, 0, tzinfo=dt.timezone.utc)

m = Map(crs=4326, figsize=(10, 5))
m.set_global()
m.coastlines()
m.land()
m.nightshade(solstice_noon)
m.set_title(f"Night at {solstice_noon:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M} UTC")
m.fig;
    solstice_noon = dt.datetime(2026, 6, 21, 12, 0, tzinfo=dt.timezone.utc) m = Map(crs=4326, figsize=(10, 5)) m.set_global() m.coastlines() m.land() m.nightshade(solstice_noon) m.set_title(f"Night at {solstice_noon:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M} UTC") m.fig;

    At the June solstice the terminator tilts hard: the Arctic is in full daylight while night reaches far over Antarctica. That tilt is the solstice — it is what produces polar day and polar night.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 8))
for ax, when in zip(axes, (solstice_noon, solstice_noon.replace(month=12, day=21))):
    panel = Map(ax=ax, crs=4326)
    panel.set_global()
    panel.coastlines()
    panel.nightshade(when)
    ax.set_title(f"{when:%d %B} 12:00 UTC")
fig;
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 8)) for ax, when in zip(axes, (solstice_noon, solstice_noon.replace(month=12, day=21))): panel = Map(ax=ax, crs=4326) panel.set_global() panel.coastlines() panel.nightshade(when) ax.set_title(f"{when:%d %B} 12:00 UTC") fig;

    The two terminators are mirror images about the equator. refraction (default -0.83°) sets the sun altitude counted as sunset — the standard allowance for atmospheric bending — and n controls how finely the curve is sampled.

    tissot — making projection distortion visible¶

    Every flat map of a sphere distorts. Tissot's indicatrices make that concrete: circles of one true ground radius, drawn where the projection puts them. Where a circle is drawn large, or as an ellipse, the map is exaggerating.

    argument meaning typical value
    lons, lats where to place the circles sequences of degrees
    radius_m true ground radius of each circle 500_000 (500 km) default
    n points per circle 64
    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    lons = [-150, -90, -30, 30, 90, 150]
lats = [-60, -30, 0, 30, 60]
grid_lons = [lon for lat in lats for lon in lons]
grid_lats = [lat for lat in lats for lon in lons]
print(f"{len(grid_lons)} indicatrices, 800 km true radius each")
    lons = [-150, -90, -30, 30, 90, 150] lats = [-60, -30, 0, 30, 60] grid_lons = [lon for lat in lats for lon in lons] grid_lats = [lat for lat in lats for lon in lons] print(f"{len(grid_lons)} indicatrices, 800 km true radius each")
    30 indicatrices, 800 km true radius each
    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    m = Map(crs=4326, figsize=(10, 5))
m.set_global()
m.coastlines()
m.tissot(grid_lons, grid_lats, radius_m=800_000)
m.set_title("Plate carrée — every circle is really 800 km across")
m.fig;
    m = Map(crs=4326, figsize=(10, 5)) m.set_global() m.coastlines() m.tissot(grid_lons, grid_lats, radius_m=800_000) m.set_title("Plate carrée — every circle is really 800 km across") m.fig;

    In plate carrée the circles keep their width in degrees but cover shrinking ground toward the poles, so the high-latitude ones are drawn far too large. That is the familiar "Greenland looks enormous" error, measured rather than asserted.

    Put the same circles on an equal-area projection and the distortion moves: areas are preserved, so the circles keep their size while their shape skews.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    m = Map(crs=3035, figsize=(7, 7))
m.coastlines()
m.tissot([0, 10, 20, 0, 10, 20], [40, 40, 40, 60, 60, 60], radius_m=200_000)
m.set_bounds([2.4e6, 1.3e6, 6.2e6, 4.6e6])   # EPSG:3035 is metres, not degrees
m.set_title("ETRS89 / LAEA Europe — equal area, shape skewed")
m.fig;
    m = Map(crs=3035, figsize=(7, 7)) m.coastlines() m.tissot([0, 10, 20, 0, 10, 20], [40, 40, 40, 60, 60, 60], radius_m=200_000) m.set_bounds([2.4e6, 1.3e6, 6.2e6, 4.6e6]) # EPSG:3035 is metres, not degrees m.set_title("ETRS89 / LAEA Europe — equal area, shape skewed") m.fig;

    This is the trade every projection makes, and tissot is how to see which trade you chose. Reach for it whenever the projection is doing real work — an area comparison, a distance claim — rather than just framing a picture.

    basemap — XYZ tiles under the map¶

    basemap() fetches raster tiles and draws them beneath everything else, in the display CRS. It needs network access; offline it is skipped rather than raising, so a notebook stays runnable either way.

    Tiles are served in Web Mercator, so EPSG:3857 is the CRS that needs no resampling — which also means set_bounds here takes metres, not degrees. Framing on the data with padding= sidesteps the conversion; passing degrees to a 3857 map silently frames a sub-metre box at Null Island, and basemap() then fetches zoom-19 tiles of the Atlantic.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    roads = FeatureCollection.read_file(str(DATA / "heidelberg_roads.geojson"))
arterials = FeatureCollection(roads[roads["klass"].isin(["trunk", "primary", "secondary"])])
print(f"{len(arterials)} arterial segments to draw over the tiles")
    roads = FeatureCollection.read_file(str(DATA / "heidelberg_roads.geojson")) arterials = FeatureCollection(roads[roads["klass"].isin(["trunk", "primary", "secondary"])]) print(f"{len(arterials)} arterial segments to draw over the tiles")
    812 arterial segments to draw over the tiles
    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    m = Map(crs=3857, figsize=(8, 8))
# Draw the data first, then frame on it: set_bounds takes DISPLAY-CRS units, and this map's are
# Web Mercator metres, not degrees. Framing on the layer avoids having to convert them by hand —
# and basemap() resolves its zoom from the framed extent, so the order matters.
m.lines(arterials, color="#b2182b", width=2.0)
m.set_bounds(padding=0.08)
m.basemap()
m.set_title("Heidelberg arterials on a tiled basemap")
m.fig;
    m = Map(crs=3857, figsize=(8, 8)) # Draw the data first, then frame on it: set_bounds takes DISPLAY-CRS units, and this map's are # Web Mercator metres, not degrees. Framing on the layer avoids having to convert them by hand — # and basemap() resolves its zoom from the framed extent, so the order matters. m.lines(arterials, color="#b2182b", width=2.0) m.set_bounds(padding=0.08) m.basemap() m.set_title("Heidelberg arterials on a tiled basemap") m.fig;

    The roads now sit on real terrain and settlement instead of white space, which is what a basemap is for: context you did not have to source or style. source= selects a provider, api_key= passes a key for the keyed ones, and preset= takes a provider dictionary.

    A caveat worth keeping: tiles are someone else's cartography, at a fixed resolution, under their licence. Check the attribution terms before publishing, and do not zoom past the level the provider serves.

    Takeaway¶

    • nightshade(when) shades the night hemisphere; pass a timezone-aware datetime.
    • tissot(lons, lats, radius_m=...) draws equal-ground-radius circles, turning projection distortion from an assertion into a measurement.
    • basemap() adds XYZ tiles underneath, best in EPSG:3857, and is skipped offline rather than failing.
    • All three decorate the globe rather than the data, so they belong under set_global() or an explicit framing.

    That closes the scene-level tour. The per-plot-type gallery is under static/.
